senses.gloss: A person paid to look after a building or piece of land.
examples: The *caretaker* plows the driveway and keeps the pipes from freezing.
We left a key with the *caretaker* of the cabin.
Two *caretakers* mow the cemetery every week.

senses.gloss: A description or portrayal that exaggerates a few traits until the subject seems ridiculous.
examples: His speech was a *caricature* of what small-town voters actually believe.
The villain is a *caricature*, not a character.
Critics said the movie reduced the whole city to a *caricature*.

senses.gloss: A fairground ride with wooden animals that go around as it turns.
examples: She rode the *carousel* four times in a row.
The park's antique *carousel* still plays organ music.
Both *carousels* at the fair had lines out to the sidewalk.

senses.gloss: The way a person holds and moves their body.
examples: You could pick out the dancer by her *carriage* alone.
He had the upright *carriage* of a former soldier.
Her *carriage* changed the moment she walked onstage.

senses.gloss: A tube holding a bullet and the powder that fires it.
examples: He loaded three *cartridges* into the rifle.
Police found a spent *cartridge* on the driveway.
The box holds fifty *cartridges*.

senses.gloss: A person or thing that is harmed or lost because of some event or decision.
examples: The music program was the first *casualty* of the budget cuts.
Privacy is often a *casualty* of new technology.
Small bookstores were the *casualties* of that merger.

senses.gloss: A person or event that causes something important to start happening.
examples: The video was the *catalyst* for months of protest.
Her arrival was the *catalyst* the team needed.
Cheap rent acted as a *catalyst* for the neighborhood's revival.

senses.gloss: A large, steep waterfall on a river.
examples: The river drops through a series of *cataracts* below the gorge.
You can hear the *cataract* a mile before you see it.
Early explorers had to carry their boats around the *cataracts*.

senses.gloss: The state of being famous.
examples: The book brought her sudden *celebrity*.
He was never comfortable with his new *celebrity*.
*Celebrity* did not make the job any easier.

senses.gloss: The most important or most noticeable part of something.
examples: Tax reform was the *centerpiece* of his campaign.
The glass wing is the *centerpiece* of the new museum.
That song is the *centerpiece* of the album.

senses.gloss: Formal manners and polite fuss on official occasions.
examples: He dropped the papers on my desk without *ceremony* and walked out.
Please don't stand on *ceremony* — just help yourself.
The old club runs on tradition and *ceremony*.

senses.gloss: A place or situation full of corruption or moral filth.
examples: He called the state capital a *cesspool* of favors and payoffs.
The comment section under that video is a *cesspool*.
She grew up hearing that the city was a *cesspool*.

senses.gloss: A formal objection questioning whether something is correct or lawful.
examples: The law faces a court *challenge* from three states.
His lawyers filed a *challenge* to the search warrant.
Both *challenges* to the election results were dismissed.

senses.gloss: A person who changes their behavior or opinions to suit whoever they are with.
examples: As a candidate he was a *chameleon*, telling each crowd what it wanted to hear.
A good salesman has to be something of a *chameleon*.
She's a social *chameleon* and fits in anywhere.

senses.gloss: Someone who publicly fights for a cause or defends other people.
examples: She was a *champion* of open records long before it was popular.
The mayor calls himself a *champion* of small business.
Farmers lost their loudest *champion* in Congress.

senses.gloss: The counter in a store where you pay for what you are buying.
examples: There were six people ahead of us at the *checkout*.
Only two *checkouts* were open on a Saturday.
She grabbed a magazine at the *checkout*.

senses.gloss: A person who loudly promotes and praises something.
examples: The paper was a *cheerleader* for the stadium deal from day one.
A manager should be a coach, not just a *cheerleader*.
The plan's *cheerleaders* ignored every warning.

senses.gloss: The natural attraction or easy connection between people.
examples: The two leads have real *chemistry* on screen.
The interview went fine, but the *chemistry* wasn't there.
This team has better *chemistry* than last year's.

senses.gloss: The code of honor and conduct that medieval knights were expected to follow.
examples: The poem celebrates *chivalry* and courtly love.
Tournaments belonged to the world of *chivalry*.
By 1500 the age of *chivalry* was over.

senses.gloss: The movement of blood around the body.
examples: Cold hands can be a sign of poor *circulation*.
Walking every day improves your *circulation*.
The bandage was so tight it cut off *circulation* to her fingers.

senses.gloss: The passing of something from person to person, or its availability for public use.
examples: Those old bills are no longer in *circulation*.
The library pulled the damaged copies out of *circulation*.
He's been sick and out of *circulation* for a month.

senses.gloss: An official notice ordering someone to pay a fine or appear in court.
examples: He got a *citation* for running the stop sign.
The restaurant received two health *citations* last year.
The officer wrote her a *citation* instead of arresting her.

senses.gloss: An official statement praising someone for bravery or achievement.
senses.ru: благодарность в приказе, награда за заслуги
examples: He received a *citation* for valor after the warehouse fire.
Her *citation* was read aloud at the ceremony.
Three officers earned *citations* that night.

senses.gloss: The way a person or organization behaves as a member of a community.
examples: Her report card gives her an A in *citizenship*.
Voting and jury duty are basic acts of *citizenship*.
The company talks a lot about corporate *citizenship*.
